stories.issue: How much macroeconomic vulnerability should India tolerate when oil shocks and US interest rates move against it?
stories.title: Oil and US rates put India’s rupee, inflation and growth trade-offs back in focus
stories.whatIsHappening: The rupee has weakened toward 96 to the dollar as Brent crude rose above $108 and US Treasury yields moved above 5%. Markets are also pricing a high probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike, increasing pressure on emerging-market currencies.
stories.argument: Allowing some currency adjustment can absorb an external shock while preserving foreign-exchange reserves, provided inflation expectations remain anchored and the move is orderly.
stories.otherSide: A weaker rupee raises the domestic cost of imported energy and other inputs. If oil remains expensive, the RBI may face pressure to keep policy tighter even when growth and investment would benefit from easier financial conditions.
stories.whyItMatters: This is not only a currency-market story. India’s oil bill, inflation, current account, bond yields, corporate margins and household purchasing power are connected through the exchange rate and energy prices.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Separate a temporary price shock from a persistent one. RBI intervention can smooth volatility but cannot permanently change the price of imported oil or the global interest-rate cycle. The policy balance depends on whether the priority is protecting purchasing power now, preserving reserves, or supporting investment and growth.
keyFacts: The rupee closed at 95.95 per dollar on September 15, its weakest level in nearly three months.
Brent crude rose above $108 a barrel and US 10-year Treasury yields crossed 5%.
The rupee had weakened for seven consecutive sessions and was down about 1.5% despite reported RBI intervention.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: If oil prices remain high, should India prioritise defending the rupee, containing inflation or protecting growth?

stories.issue: Should governments accept higher trade costs in exchange for strategic resilience and policy autonomy?
stories.title: The WTO warns that trade fragmentation could leave everyone poorer
stories.whatIsHappening: A new WTO analysis models the economic cost of a world divided into competing geopolitical blocs and warns that tariffs, subsidies and export controls are putting the rules-based trading system under strain.
stories.argument: Some trade restrictions can be justified where supply security, national security or resilience matters more than lowest-cost sourcing. Regional and sector-specific agreements can also be useful when global consensus is difficult.
stories.otherSide: Broad tariff escalation and competing blocs can reduce scale, raise prices and divert production away from the most efficient locations. Retaliation also makes it harder for smaller and poorer economies to benefit from trade.
stories.whyItMatters: India is trying to expand manufacturing and exports while negotiating more trade agreements. The central strategic question is whether protection and diversification will build capability or make Indian firms less competitive and the global economy less predictable.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Do not treat openness and resilience as complete opposites. Targeted protection may insure against catastrophic disruption, but permanent protection can preserve inefficiency. Ask which sectors are genuinely strategic, who pays the higher cost, and whether support has a clear path toward competitiveness.
keyFacts: The WTO modelling says a world split into geopolitical blocs could have global GDP 5.1% lower and exports 18.6% lower by 2050 than a more cooperative baseline.
In a more severe patchwork of free-trade agreements, the modelled losses rise to 6.9% of GDP and nearly 27% of exports.
About 72% of global merchandise trade still takes place under WTO most-favoured-nation terms, down from roughly 80% in 2022.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: When does supply-chain resilience become inefficient protectionism?

stories.issue: Can India sustain high growth if private investment and job creation do not take over from public spending?
stories.title: India’s next growth phase depends on whether private capital steps up
stories.whatIsHappening: Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran argued that policy cannot be the only engine of growth and called on private companies to invest, hire, pay fairly and increase research spending. Investment in the June quarter was reported to be 11.9% higher than a year earlier.
stories.argument: Public capital expenditure can create infrastructure and crowd in private investment, but sustained productivity, employment and innovation require businesses to take more risk and expand capacity themselves.
stories.otherSide: Private investment will remain cautious if demand, regulation, financing costs and global trade conditions are uncertain. Asking firms to invest without fixing these constraints can shift responsibility from policy makers to companies without solving the underlying problem.
stories.whyItMatters: India’s growth model has implications for employment, manufacturing, exports, productivity and fiscal sustainability. It also affects whether the country can turn its demographic scale into rising incomes rather than underemployment.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Public and private investment are complements, not substitutes. Government spending can improve logistics and reduce risk, while firms determine whether that capacity becomes productive jobs and competitive exports. The useful test is whether reforms, infrastructure and demand conditions make productive private investment more attractive than financial caution or short-term consumption.
keyFacts: Investment in the June quarter was reported as 11.9% higher year on year.
The CEA said public policy cannot be the only instrument driving the economy and called for higher private-sector investment and R&D.
The article links India’s UK and EU trade agreements with opportunities for labour-intensive export sectors.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: What should India change first if it wants private investment to create more productive jobs: regulation, infrastructure, skills or demand?

stories.issue: Can attacks on economic infrastructure change the strategic balance of a war, or mainly impose civilian costs?
stories.title: Russia’s infrastructure war is turning military pressure into an economic test
stories.whatIsHappening: Le Monde reports that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, ports and other infrastructure are adding pressure to an economy already shaped by war spending, labour shortages and high interest rates. The attacks have become part of a broader contest over fuel, government revenue and public morale.
stories.argument: Targeting economically important infrastructure can raise the cost of war, reduce energy-processing capacity and expose vulnerabilities that conventional battlefield measures may not capture.
stories.otherSide: Infrastructure attacks can produce inflation, shortages and civilian hardship without guaranteeing a political or military breakthrough. They can also intensify escalation risks and strengthen the case for greater state control and mobilisation.
stories.whyItMatters: The conflict affects energy markets, defence spending, sanctions, food and commodity security, and the ability of governments to finance prolonged wars. It is a useful case study in how national resilience is measured beyond GDP growth.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: A wartime economy can show headline resilience while accumulating distortions: defence spending may support output even as civilian investment and welfare weaken. Assess whether attacks change the opponent’s capacity, fiscal position and public tolerance, rather than assuming that economic damage automatically changes battlefield outcomes.
keyFacts: The report says Ukrainian strikes reduced Russia’s oil-processing capacity by about 20% to 30%.
Defence spending is described as more than 8% of Russian GDP and about 40% of government spending, compared with about 5% of GDP before the invasion.
Russia’s 2026 GDP growth is expected in the report to be no more than 1%, while inflation had moved above 6%.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: How should governments and businesses assess resilience when a conflict targets the economic infrastructure behind everyday life?

stories.issue: Should leading AI companies slow frontier development when safety risks are uncertain but competitive pressure is intense?
stories.title: AI leaders agree on slowing down—but not on how to make that possible
stories.whatIsHappening: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, xAI’s Elon Musk and other AI leaders have recently supported slowing the development of the most advanced systems amid concerns about misuse and loss of control. The debate has also unsettled technology markets and exposed disagreement over how voluntary restraint could work.
stories.argument: A pause or slower frontier race could give regulators, researchers and companies more time to test systems, develop safeguards and establish clearer accountability before deployment becomes harder to reverse.
stories.otherSide: Voluntary slowing is difficult when firms and countries fear losing technological and economic advantage. A slowdown could also delay beneficial applications and leave safety standards to be set by less transparent competitors.
stories.whyItMatters: This is simultaneously a technology-governance, labour-market, capital-allocation and national-competitiveness question. India’s large IT-services sector is exposed to both the productivity opportunity and the risk that AI changes the business model faster than workers can adapt.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Distinguish slowing frontier capability from stopping useful deployment. The practical questions are who defines an acceptable risk, how compliance is verified, whether rules apply across borders, and whether investment should shift from larger models toward reliability, evaluation and adoption. Safety arguments are stronger when they specify measurable thresholds rather than relying only on catastrophic scenarios.
keyFacts: Reuters reported India’s IT industry at about $315 billion and said its IT index was down about 21% during 2026 at the time of the report.
The same report said Indian IT stocks rose as much as 5.2% after calls for slower AI development.
The AP report described competition, profit incentives and political resistance as obstacles to coordinated restraint.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: Would a slower AI race improve social outcomes, or would it mainly shift the advantage to competitors that do not slow down?

extempore.issue: Should India accept higher trade costs and less efficiency in exchange for supply-chain resilience and strategic autonomy?
extempore.whyNow: A new WTO analysis has quantified the cost of a world divided into competing trade blocs, while India is simultaneously trying to expand manufacturing, attract private investment and protect itself from energy and geopolitical shocks.
argumentsFor: Strategic sectors such as energy, semiconductors and critical inputs can justify paying for redundancy because disruption costs may be much larger than the efficiency loss.
Domestic capability and diversified suppliers can give India more bargaining power and reduce dependence on any single country or bloc.
Targeted industrial policy can create learning, jobs and export capacity if support is tied to productivity and global competitiveness.
argumentsAgainst: Broad tariffs and duplicated capacity raise costs for consumers and businesses and can make Indian exports less competitive.
Retaliation and competing trade blocs can reduce market access, especially for developing economies that need open trade to scale.
Protection can become permanent if politically connected firms benefit without becoming efficient, turning resilience into expensive self-sufficiency.
examples: The WTO’s modelling of lower global GDP and exports under geopolitical trade fragmentation.
India’s effort to build electronics and semiconductor capacity while negotiating trade agreements and keeping multiple strategic relationships open.
facts: The WTO modelled a 5.1% fall in global GDP and an 18.6% fall in exports by 2050 under geopolitical fragmentation relative to a cooperative baseline.
About 72% of global merchandise trade still uses WTO most-favoured-nation terms.
India’s private investment and export ambitions make the cost of imported inputs and market access especially important.
extempore.structure: Opening → Define resilience versus efficiency → Argument 1 → Argument 2 → Counterargument → India-specific position → Conclusion
